name: Iron City No. 1 Power Generator and Compute Center

profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap point, tagged telecom=data_center and named "Iron City No.1 Power Generator and Compute Center," describes a facility that pairs on-site electricity generation with computing hardware. That combination, generation plus compute co-located behind the meter, is the standard architecture for cryptocurrency mining operations rather than for conventional enterprise colocation or cloud data centers, which normally draw power from the regional utility grid instead of running their own generators. Bitcoin miners in particular have increasingly sought out stranded or otherwise underused power sources, including natural gas wells that would otherwise flare excess gas, because mining rigs can absorb power output that has no other nearby buyer and can be throttled up or down with the availability of that power. Pennsylvania has seen several such projects sited near natural gas infrastructure in the Marcellus Shale region. Public reporting and an operator website naming this specific site's owner, generation fuel source, and mining hardware count could not be located this session, so this entry records the facility's self-described function rather than a fully sourced operational profile. It should be read as a cryptocurrency mining and compute hosting site rather than as a general-purpose enterprise data center, and updated if a named operator or additional public documentation becomes available.

reading.body:
Iron City No. 1's name and architecture indicate it is a behind-the-meter power generation and compute facility, the standard design for cryptocurrency mining operations rather than cloud or enterprise colocation. The facility pairs on-site electricity generation with computing hardware, a configuration suited to absorbing stranded or flared power that has no other nearby buyer, a pattern common in Pennsylvania's natural gas infrastructure regions. No operator name, generation source, generation capacity, or computing hardware specifications are published.

The facility's published power specifications, operator identity, and current operational status could not be located. Pennsylvania has 14 mapped data center facilities and only 4 with published power figures totaling 22.2 MW. This entry ranks fifth by published capacity in the state, though that ranking is provisional and reflects only the four facilities with disclosed specifications. Until an operator website or public reporting discloses the site's generation source and compute load, its actual scale and role in AI infrastructure cannot be quantified.

For a reader assessing whether this facility matters to AI scaling, the absence of published specifications makes it impossible to measure its contribution to available compute capacity or grid demand. The behind-the-meter mining architecture suggests it may use power sources unavailable to conventional data centers, but without disclosure of MW or rack count, its significance to state or national AI infrastructure cannot be determined from public sources.
